entries.4b164ecd8b5a9a522a5901306a65b794bb156609: <div sID="gen32379" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Tim.2" sID="1Tim.2"/> <div eID="gen32379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32380" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32381" type="x-p"/> In this chapter Paul treats, I. Of prayer, with many reasons for it, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1-1Tim.2.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. Of women's apparel, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. III. Of their subjection, with the reasons of it, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.14">ver. 11-14</reference>. IV. A promise given for their encouragement in child-bearing, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.15">ver. 15</reference>.
entries.306c4ca1b787d2b1f65924823cf2545f3c22abba: <div eID="gen32381" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32380" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Universal Prayer Recommended. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32382" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, <hi type="italic">and</hi> giving of thanks, be made for all men; <hi type="super">2</hi> For kings, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. <hi type="super">3</hi> For this <hi type="italic">is</hi> good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; <hi type="super">4</hi> Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. 5 For <hi type="italic">there is</hi> one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; <hi type="super">6</hi> Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time. <hi type="super">7</hi> Whereunto I am ordained a preacher, and an apostle, (I speak the truth in Christ, <hi type="italic">and</hi> lie not;) a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and verity. 8 I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting. <div eID="gen32382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32383" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A charge given to Christians to pray for all men in general, and particularly for all in authority. Timothy must take care that this be done. Paul does not send him any prescribed form of prayer, as we have reason to think he would if he had intended that ministers should be tied to that way of praying; but, in general, that they should make <hi type="italic">supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks:</hi> supplications for the averting of evil, prayers for the obtaining of good, intercessions for others, and thanksgivings for mercies already received. Paul thought it enough to give them general heads; they, having the scripture to direct them in prayer and the Spirit of prayer poured out upon them, needed not any further directions. Observe, The design of the Christian religion is to promote prayer; and the disciples of Christ must be praying people. Pray <hi type="italic">always with all prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Eph. vi. 18</reference>. There must be prayers for ourselves in the first place; this is implied here. We must also pray <hi type="italic">for all men,</hi> for the world of mankind in general, for particular persons who need or desire our prayers. See how far the Christian religion was from being a sect, when it taught men this diffusive charity, to pray, not only for those of their own way, but for all men. Pray for kings (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.2">v. 2</reference>); though the kings at this time were heathens, enemies to Christianity, and persecutors of Christians, yet they must pray for them, because it is for the public good that there should be civil government, and proper persons entrusted with the administration of it, for whom therefore we ought to pray, yea, though we ourselves suffer under them. <hi type="italic">For kings, and all that are in authority,</hi> that is, inferior magistrates: we must pray for them, and we must give thanks for them, pray for their welfare and for the welfare of their kingdoms, and therefore must not plot against them, that in the peace thereof we may have peace, and give thanks for them and for the benefit we have under their government, that <hi type="italic">we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.</hi> Here see what we must desire for kings, that God will so turn their hearts, and direct them and make use of them, that we under them may lead a quiet and peaceable life. He does not say, "that we may get preferments under them, grow rich, and be in honour and power under them;" no, the summit of the ambition of a good Christian is to lead a quiet and peaceable life, to get through the world unmolested in a low private station. We should desire that we and others may lead a peaceable life <hi type="italic">in all godliness and honesty,</hi> implying that we cannot expect to be kept quiet and peaceable unless we keep in all godliness and honesty. Let us mind our duty, and then we may expect to be taken under the protection both of God and the government. <hi type="italic">In all godliness and honesty.</hi> Here we have our duty as Christians summed up in two words: godliness, that is, the right worshipping of God; and honesty, that is, a good conduct towards all men. These two must go together; we are not truly honest if we are not godly, and do not render to God his due; and we are not truly godly if we are not honest, for God hates robbery for burnt-offering. Here we may observe, 1. Christians are to be men much given to prayer: they ought to abound herein, and should use themselves to prayers, supplications, &c. 2. In our prayers we are to have a generous concern for others as well as for ourselves; we are to pray for all men, and to give thanks for all men; and must not confine our prayers nor thanksgiving to our own persons or families. 3. Prayer consists of various parts, of supplications, intercessions, and thanksgivings; for we must pray for the mercies we want, as well as be thankful for mercies already received; and we are to deprecate the judgments which our own sins or the sins of others have deserved. 4. All men, yea, kings themselves, and those who are in authority, are to be prayed for. They want our prayers, for they have many difficulties to encounter, many snares to which their exalted stations expose them. 5. In praying for our governors, we take the most likely course to lead a peaceable and quiet life. The Jews at Babylon were commanded to seek the peace of the city whither the Lord had caused them to be carried captives, and to pray to the Lord for it; for in the peace thereof they should have peace, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jer. xxix. 7</reference>. 6. If we would lead a peaceable and quiet life, we must live in all godliness and honesty; we must do our duty to God and man. <hi type="italic">He that will love life, and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile; let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and pursue it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.10-1Pet.3.11">1 Pet. iii. 10, 11</reference>. Now the reason he gives for this is <hi type="italic">because this is good in the sight of God our Saviour;</hi> that is, the gospel of Christ requires this. That which is acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour we should do, and should abound in. <div eID="gen32383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32384" type="x-p"/> II. As a reason why we should in our prayers concern ourselves for all men, he shows God's love to mankind in general, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen32384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32385" type="x-p"/> 1. One reason why all men are to be prayed for is because there is one God, and that God bears a good will to all mankind. There is one God (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">v. 5</reference>), and one only, there is no other, there can be no other, for there can be but one infinite. This one God <hi type="italic">will have all men to be saved;</hi> he desires not the death and destruction of any (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.11">Ezek. xxxiii. 11</reference>), but the welfare and salvation of all. Not that he has decreed the salvation of all, for then all men would be saved; but he has a good will to the salvation of all, and none perish but by their own fault, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>. He will have all to be saved, <hi type="italic">and to come to the knowledge of the truth,</hi> to be saved in the way that he has appointed and not otherwise. It concerns us to get the knowledge of the truth, because that is the way to be saved; <hi type="italic">Christ is the way and the truth, and so he is the life.</hi> <div eID="gen32385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32386" type="x-p"/> 2. There is one Mediator, and that mediator gave himself a ransom for all. As the mercy of God extends itself to all his works, so the mediation of Christ extends itself thus far to all the children of men that he paid a price sufficient for the salvation of all mankind; he brought mankind to stand upon new terms with God, so that they are not now under the law as a covenant of works, but as a rule of life. They are under grace; not under the covenant of innocence, but under a new covenant: <hi type="italic">He gave himself a ransom.</hi> Observe, The death of Christ was a ransom, a counter-price. We deserved to have died. Christ died for us, to save us from death and hell; he gave himself a ransom voluntarily, a ransom for all; so that all mankind are put in a better condition than that of devils. He died to work out a common salvation: in order hereunto, he put himself into the office of Mediator between God and man. A mediator supposes a controversy. Sin had made a quarrel between us and God; Jesus Christ is a Mediator who undertakes to make peace, to bring God and man together, in the nature of an umpire or arbitrator, a days-man who lays his hand upon u both, <reference osisRef="Job.9.33">Job ix. 33</reference>. He is a ransom that <hi type="italic">was to be testified in due time;</hi> that is, in the Old-Testament times, his sufferings and the glory that should follow were spoken of as things to be revealed in the last times, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 10, 11</reference>. And they are accordingly revealed, Paul himself having been ordained a preacher and an apostle, to publish to the Gentiles the glad tidings of redemption and salvation by Jesus Christ. This doctrine of Christ's mediation Paul was entrusted to preach to every creature, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.15">Mark xvi. 15</reference>. He was appointed to be a teacher of the Gentiles; besides his general call to the apostleship, he was commissioned particularly to preach to the Gentiles, <hi type="italic">in faith and truth,</hi> or faithfully and truly. Note, (1.) It is good and acceptable in the sight of God and our Saviour that we pray for kings and for all men, and also that we lead a peaceable and quiet life; and this is a very good reason why we should do the one as well as the other. (2.) God has a good will to the salvation of all; so that it is not so much the want of a will in God to save them as it is a want of will in themselves to be saved in God's way. Here our blessed Lord charges the fault: <hi type="italic">You will not come unto me that you may have life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.40">John v. 40</reference>. <hi type="italic">I would have gathered you, and you would not.</hi> (3.) Those who are saved must come to the knowledge of the truth, for this is God's appointed way to save sinners. Without knowledge the heart cannot be good; if we do not know the truth, we cannot be ruled by it. (4.) It is observable that the unity of God is asserted, and joined with the unity of the Mediator; and the church of Rome might as well maintain a plurality of gods as a plurality of mediators. (5.) He that is a Mediator in the New-Testament sense, gave himself a ransom. Vain then is the pretence of the Romanists that there is but one Mediator of satisfaction, but many of intercession; for, according to Paul, Christ's giving himself a ransom was a necessary part of the Mediator's office; and indeed this lays the foundation for his intercession. (6.) Paul was ordained a minister, to declare this to the Gentiles, that Christ is the one Mediator between God and men, who gave himself a ransom for all. This is the substance of which all ministers are to preach, to the end of the world; and Paul magnified his office, as he was the apostle of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.13">Rom. xi. 13</reference>. (7.) Ministers must preach the truth, what they apprehend to be so, and they must believe it themselves; they are, like our apostle, to preach in faith and verity, and they must also be faithful and trusty. <div eID="gen32386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32387" type="x-p"/> III. A direction how to pray, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">v. 8</reference>. 1. Now, under the gospel, prayer is not to be confined to any one particular house of prayer, but men must pray every where: no place is amiss for prayer, no place more acceptable to God than another, <reference osisRef="John.4.21">John iv. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Pray every where.</hi> We must pray in our closets, pray in our families, pray at our meals, pray when we are on journeys, and pray in the solemn assemblies, whether more public or private. 2. It is the will of God that in prayer we should lift up holy hands: <hi type="italic">Lifting up holy hands,</hi> or pure hands, pure from the pollution of sin, washed in the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness. <hi type="italic">I will wash my hands,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>. 3. We must pray in charity: <hi type="italic">Without wrath,</hi> or malice, or anger at any person. 4. We must pray in faith <hi type="italic">without doubting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jam. i. 6</reference>), or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">without disputing,</hi> and then it falls under the head of charity.
entries.9e6911feb953265c16e74a186fdd0490d26bbdf5: <div eID="gen32387" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Charge to Females. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32388" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; <hi type="super">10</hi> But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works. 11 Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. 12 But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. <hi type="super">13</hi> For Adam was first formed, then Eve. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression. <hi type="super">15</hi> Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety. <div eID="gen32388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32389" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a charge, that women who profess the Christian religion should be modest, sober, silent, and submissive, as becomes their place. 1. They must be very modest in their apparel, not affecting gaudiness, gaiety, or costliness (you may read the vanity of a person's mind in the gaiety and gaudiness of his habit), because they have better ornaments with which they should <hi type="italic">adorn themselves, with good works.</hi> Note, Good works are the best ornament; these are, in the sight of God, of great price. Those that profess godliness should, in their dress, as well as other things, act as becomes their profession; instead of laying out their money on fine clothes, they must lay it out in works of piety and charity, which are properly called good works. 2. Women must learn the principles of their religion, learn Christ, learn the scriptures; they must not think that their sex excuses them from that learning which is necessary to salvation. 3. They must be silent, submissive, and subject, and not usurp authority. The reason given is because <hi type="italic">Adam was first formed, then Eve</hi> out of him, to denote her subordination to him and dependence upon him; and that she was made for him, to be a help-meet for him. And as she was last in the creation, which is one reason for her subjection, so she was first in the transgression, and that is another reason. <hi type="italic">Adam was not deceived,</hi> that is, not first; the serpent did not immediately set upon him, but the woman was first in the transgression (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.3">2 Cor. xi. 3</reference>), and it was part of the sentence, <hi type="italic">Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>. But it is a word of comfort (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.15">v. 15</reference>) that those who continue in sobriety shall be <hi type="italic">saved in child-bearing,</hi> or <hi type="italic">with</hi> child-bearing—the Messiah, who was born of a woman, should break the serpent's head (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>); or the sentence which they are under for sin shall be no bar to their acceptance with Christ, <hi type="italic">if they continue in faith, and charity, and holiness, with sobriety.</hi> <div eID="gen32389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32390" type="x-p"/> II. Here observe, 1. The extensiveness of the rules of Christianity; they reach not only to men, but to women, not only to their persons, but also to their dress, which must be modest, like their sex; and to their outward deportment and behaviour, it must be in silence, with all subjection. 2. Women are to profess godliness as well as men; for they are baptized, and thereby stand engaged to exercise themselves to godliness; and, to their honour be it spoken, many of them were eminent professors of Christianity in the days of the apostles, as the book of Acts will inform us. 3. Women being more in danger of exceeding in their apparel, it was more necessary to caution them in this respect. 4. The best ornaments for professors of godliness are good works. 5. According to Paul, women must be learners, and are not allowed to be public teachers in the church; for teaching is an office of authority, and the woman must not usurp authority over the man, but is to be in silence. But, notwithstanding this prohibition, good women may and ought to teach their children at home the principles of religion. Timothy from a child had known the holy scriptures; and who should teach him but his mother and grandmother? <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2 Tim. iii. 15</reference>. Aquila and his wife Priscilla expounded unto Apollos the way of God more perfectly; but then they did it privately, for <hi type="italic">they took him unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.18.26">Acts xviii. 26</reference>. 6. Here are two very good reasons given for the man's authority over the woman, and her subjection to the man, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.13-1Tim.2.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Adam was first formed, then Eve; she was created for the man, and not the man for the woman (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9">1 Cor. xi. 9</reference>); then she was deceived, and brought the man into the transgression. 7. Though the difficulties and dangers of childbearing are many and great, as they are part of the punishment inflicted on the sex for Eve's transgression, yet here is much for her support and encouragement: <hi type="italic">Notwithstanding she shall be saved,</hi> &c. Though in sorrow, yet she shall bring forth, and be a living mother of living children; with this proviso, that they continue in faith, and charity, and holiness, with sobriety: and women, under the circumstance of child-bearing should by faith lay hold of this promise for their support in the needful time.  <chapter eID="1Tim.2"/> <div eID="gen32390" type="x-p"/>

entries.fdc382abeb06b1ad22e70e30eb9e11a1f3d5f314: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18076"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen37158" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1-1Tim.2.15">1Ti 2:1-15</reference>. Public Worship. Direction as to Intercessions for All Men, since Christ Is a Ransom for All. The Duties of Men and Women Respectively in Respect to Public Prayer. Woman's Subjection; Her Sphere of Duty.<div eID="gen37158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18076"/><hi type="bold">1. therefore--</hi>taking up again the general subject of the Epistle in continuation (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">2Ti 2:1</reference>). "What I have therefore to say to thee by way of a charge (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>), is," &c.<div eID="gen37159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that, first of all ... be made--</hi>Alford takes it, "I exhort first of all to make." "First of all," doubtless, is to be connected with "I exhort"; what I begin with (for special reasons), is ... As the destruction of Jerusalem drew near, the Jews (including those at Ephesus) were seized with the dream of freedom from every yoke; and so virtually "'blasphemed" (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>) God's name by "speaking evil of dignities" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">1Ti 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.10">2Pe 2:10</reference>; Jude 8). Hence Paul, in opposition, gives prominence to the injunction that prayer be made for all men, especially for magistrates and kings (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.1-Titus.3.3">Tit 3:1-3</reference>) [Olshausen]. Some professing Christians looked down on all not Christians, as doomed to perdition; but Paul says all men are to be prayed for, as Christ died for all (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4-1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:4-6</reference>).<div eID="gen37160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">supplications--</hi>a term implying the suppliant's sense of need, and of his own insufficiency.<div eID="gen37161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prayers--</hi>implying devotion.<div eID="gen37162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">intercessions--</hi>properly the coming near to God with childlike confidence, generally in behalf of another. The accumulation of terms implies prayer in its every form and aspect, according to all the relations implied in it. <div eID="gen37163" type="x-p"/>
entries.926d5ce544c2d1cd557e7c75e5f4906275000027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18077"/><div sID="gen37164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18077"/><hi type="bold">2. For kings--</hi>an effectual confutation of the adversaries who accused the Christians of disaffection to the ruling powers (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">Ac 17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.7">Ro 13:1-7</reference>).<div eID="gen37164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... in authority--</hi>literally, "in eminence"; in stations of eminence. The "quiet" of Christians was often more dependent on subordinate rulers, than on the supreme king; hence, "all ... in authority" are to be prayed for.<div eID="gen37165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we may lead--</hi>that we may be blessed with such good government as to lead ... ; or rather, as Greek, "to pass" or "spend." The prayers of Christians for the government bring down from heaven peace and order in a state.<div eID="gen37166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quiet--</hi>not troubled from without.<div eID="gen37167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peaceable--</hi>"tranquil"; not troubled from within [Olshausen]. "He is peaceable (Greek) who makes no disturbance; he is quiet (Greek) who is himself free from disturbance" [Tittmann].<div eID="gen37168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all godliness--</hi>"in all (possible ... requisite) piety" [Alford]. A distinct Greek word, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.10">1Ti 2:10</reference>, expresses "godliness."<div eID="gen37169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honesty--</hi>Greek, "gravity" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.2">Tit 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>), "decorum," or propriety of conduct. As "piety" is in relation to God, "gravity" is propriety of behavior among men. In the Old Testament the Jews were commanded to pray for their heathen rulers (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.10">Ezr 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jr 29:7</reference>). The Jews, by Augustus' order, offered a lamb daily for the Roman emperor, till near the destruction of Jerusalem. The Jewish Zealots, instigated by Eleazar, caused this custom to cease [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 2.17], whence the war originated, according to Josephus. <div eID="gen37170" type="x-p"/>
entries.717a345fb2e59658e9f3c2f92f849e350c9091c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18078"/><div sID="gen37171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18078"/><hi type="bold">3. this--</hi>praying for all men.<div eID="gen37171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sight of God--</hi>not merely before men, as if it were their favor that we sought (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.21">2Co 8:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our Saviour--</hi>a title appropriate to the matter in hand. He who is "our Saviour" is willing that all should be saved (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference>); therefore we should meet the will of God in behalf of others, by praying for the salvation of all men. More would be converted if we would pray more. He has actually saved us who believe, being "our Saviour." He is willing that all should be saved, even those who do not as yet believe, if they will believe (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37173" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a88a6e0b555ff37e46cc88b4bc97e5d2a0b3808: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18079"/><div sID="gen37174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18079"/>4. "Imitate God." Since He wishes that all should be saved, do you also wish it; and if you wish it, pray for it. For prayer is the instrument of effecting such things [Chrysostom]. Paul does not say, "He wishes to save all"; for then he would have saved all in matter of fact; but "will have all men to be saved," implies the possibility of man's accepting it (through God's prevenient grace) or rejecting it (through man's own perversity). Our prayers ought to include all, as God's grace included all.<div eID="gen37174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to come--</hi>They are not forced.<div eID="gen37175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the knowledge--</hi>Greek, "the full knowledge" or "recognition" (See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.9">Php 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the truth--</hi>the saving truth as it is in, and by, Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen37177" type="x-p"/>
entries.89f611996014cd7cdf7f8c5fb0963d7f6b1d5c23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18080"/><div sID="gen37178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18080"/><hi type="bold">5. For there is one God--</hi>God's unity in essence and purpose is a proof of His comprehending all His human children alike (created in His image) in His offer of grace (compare the same argument from His unity, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.30">Ro 3:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.20">Ga 3:20</reference>); therefore all are to be prayed for. <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference> is proved from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>, from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>. The one God is common to all (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Is 45:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Ac 17:26</reference>). The one Mediator is mediator between God and all men potentially (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">Ro 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.5">Ep 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.6">He 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">12:24</reference>). They who have not this one God by one Mediator, have none: literally, a "go-between." The Greek order is not "and one mediator," but "one mediator also between ... While God will have all men to be saved by knowing God and the Mediator, there is a legitimate, holy order in the exercise of that will wherewith men ought to receive it. All mankind constitute, as it were, ONE MAN before God [Bengel].<div eID="gen37178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man--</hi>rather "man," absolutely and genetically: not a mere individual man: the Second Head of humanity, representing and embodying in Himself the whole human race and nature. There is no "the" in the Greek. This epithet is thus the strongest corroboration of his argument, namely, that Christ's mediation affects the whole race, since there is but the one Mediator, designed as the Representative Man for all men alike (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1Co 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.14">Col 2:14</reference>). His being "man" was necessary to His being a Mediator, sympathizing with us through experimental knowledge of our nature (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Is 50:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">4:15</reference>). Even in nature, almost all blessings are conveyed to us from God, not immediately, but through the mediation of various agents. The effectual intercession of Moses for Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.14.13-Num.14.19">Nu 14:13-19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.29">De 9:1-29</reference>); of Abraham for Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Ge 20:7</reference>); of Job for his friends (<reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>), the mediation being PRESCRIBED by God while declaring His purposes of forgiveness: all prefigure the grand mediation for all by the one Mediator. On the other hand, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference> asserts that He was also God. <div eID="gen37179" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7dd52cf2201a5f862c0dc42ef0ddda653573939: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18081"/><div sID="gen37180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18081"/><hi type="bold">6. gave himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>). Not only the Father gave Him for us (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>); but the Son gave Himself (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.5-Phil.2.8">Php 2:5-8</reference>).<div eID="gen37180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ransom--</hi>properly of a captive slave. Man was the captive slave of Satan, sold under sin. He was unable to ransom himself, because absolute obedience is due to God, and therefore no act of ours can satisfy for the least offense. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.48">Le 25:48</reference> allowed one sold captive to be redeemed by one of his brethren. The Son of God, therefore, became man in order that, being made like unto us in all things, sin only excepted, as our elder brother He should redeem us (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>). The Greek implies not merely ransom, but a substituted or equivalent ransom: the Greek preposition, "anti," implying reciprocity and vicarious substitution.<div eID="gen37181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for all--</hi>Greek, "in behalf of all": not merely for a privileged few; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>: the argument for praying in behalf of all is given here.<div eID="gen37182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be testified--</hi>Greek, "the testimony (that which was to be testified of, <reference osisRef="1John.5.8-1John.5.11">1Jo 5:8-11</reference>) in its own due times," or seasons, that is, in the times appointed by God for its being testified of (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>). The oneness of the Mediator, involving the universality of redemption (which faith, however, alone appropriates), was the great subject of Christian testimony [Alford] (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">1Co 1:6</reference>; 2:1; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen37183" type="x-p"/>
entries.9be8422f22ed83d4b5c20ac26c820ea19f668c5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18082"/><div sID="gen37184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18082"/><hi type="bold">7. Whereunto--</hi>For the giving of which testimony.<div eID="gen37184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am ordained--</hi>literally, "I was set": the same Greek, as "putting me," &c. (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1Ti 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preacher--</hi>literally, "herald" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.11">15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.11">2Ti 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>). He recurs to himself, as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>, in himself a living pattern or announcement of the Gospel, so here "a herald and teacher of (it to) the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Ga 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1-Eph.3.12">Ep 3:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>). The universality of his commission is an appropriate assertion here, where he is arguing to prove that prayers are to be made "for all men" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I speak the truth ... and lie not--</hi>a strong asseveration of his universal commission, characteristic of the ardor of the apostle, exposed to frequent conflict (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Ro 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in faith and verity--</hi>rather, "in the faith and the truth." The sphere in which his ministry was appointed to be exercised was the faith and the truth (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>): the Gospel truth, the subject matter of the faith [Wiesinger]. <div eID="gen37188" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e6eaffe30107af61fca4e30c1be95ea3fbb3fd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18083"/><div sID="gen37189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18083"/><hi type="bold">8. I will--</hi>The active wish, or desire, is meant.<div eID="gen37189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that men--</hi>rather as Greek, "that the men," as distinguished from "the women," to whom he has something different to say from what he said to the men (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.12">1Ti 2:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.14">1Co 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>). The emphasis, however, is not on this, but on the precept of praying, resumed from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>.<div eID="gen37190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everywhere--</hi>Greek, "in every place," namely, of public prayer. Fulfilling Mal 1:11, "In every place ... from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same ... incense shall be offered unto My name"; and Jesus' words, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.20">Mt 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.21">Joh 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.23">23</reference>.<div eID="gen37191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifting up holy hands--</hi>The early Christians turned up their palms towards heaven, as those craving help do. So also Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.22">1Ki 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>). The Jews washed their hands before prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Psa 26:6</reference>). Paul figuratively (compare <reference osisRef="Job.17.9">Job 17:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">Jas 4:8</reference>) uses language alluding to this custom here: so <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>. The Greek for "holy" means hands which have committed no impiety, and observed every sacred duty. This (or at least the contrite desire to be so) is a needful qualification for effectual prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">Psa 24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen37192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without wrath--</hi>putting it away (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.23">Mt 5:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.15">6:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doubting--</hi>rather, "disputing," as the Greek is translated in <reference osisRef="Phil.2.14">Php 2:14</reference>. Such things hinder prayer (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.46">Lu 9:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1">Ro 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>). Bengel supports English Version (compare an instance, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.2">2Ki 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.14.31">Mt 14:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.11.22-Mark.11.24">Mr 11:22-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen37194" type="x-p"/>
entries.21b466f0457fe0b88c3f54f1086c92a1bcd726e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18084"/><div sID="gen37195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18084"/>9-10. The context requires that we understand these directions as to women, in relation to their deportment in public worship, though the rules will hold good on other occasions also.<div eID="gen37195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in modest apparel--</hi>"in seemly guise" [Ellicott]. The adjective means properly. orderly, decorous, becoming; the noun in secular writings means conduct, bearing. But here "apparel." Women are apt to love fine dress; and at Ephesus the riches of some (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>) would lead them to dress luxuriously. The Greek in <reference osisRef="Titus.2.3">Tit 2:3</reference> is a more general term meaning "deportment."<div eID="gen37196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shamefacedness--</hi>Trench spells this word according to its true derivation, "shamefastness" (that which is made fast by an honorable shame); as "steadfastness" (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen37197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sobriety--</hi>"self-restraint" [Alford]. Habitual inner self-government [Trench]. I prefer Ellicott's translation, "sober-mindedness": the well-balanced state of mind arising from habitual self-restraint.<div eID="gen37198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>Greek, "in."<div eID="gen37199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">braided hair--</hi>literally, "plaits," that is, plaited hair: probably with the "gold and pearls" intertwined (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3">1Pe 3:3</reference>). Such gaud is characteristic of the spiritual harlot (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.4">Re 17:4</reference>). <div eID="gen37200" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ffd0880dbab68c9f50d979f21aad5b22921ae6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18086"/><div sID="gen37203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18086"/><hi type="bold">11. learn--</hi>not "teach" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1Ti 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>). She should not even put questions in the public assembly (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">1Co 14:35</reference>).<div eID="gen37203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with all subjection--</hi>not "usurping authority" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1Ti 2:12</reference>). She might teach, but not in public (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.26">Ac 18:26</reference>). Paul probably wrote this Epistle from Corinth, where the precept (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>) was in force. <div eID="gen37204" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1a35dfae0dcba739239fb15eafdf512cc86bbbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18087"/><div sID="gen37205" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18087"/><hi type="bold">12. usurp authority--</hi>"to lord it over the man" [Alford], literally, "to be an autocrat." <div eID="gen37205" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c1df154298a74d11e64319397895c6d09e6ef3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18088"/><div sID="gen37206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18088"/><hi type="bold">13. For--</hi>reason of the precept; the original order of creation.<div eID="gen37206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Adam ... first--</hi>before Eve, who was created for him (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.8">1Co 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen37207" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb4fbd76c0b34b1ffbad79f11502c5eff580075a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18089"/><div sID="gen37208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18089"/><hi type="bold">14. Adam was not deceived--</hi>as Eve was deceived by the serpent; but was persuaded by his wife. <reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Ge 3:17</reference>, "hearkened unto ... voice of ... wife." But in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.13">Ge 3:13</reference>, Eve says, "The serpent beguiled me." Being more easily deceived, she more easily deceives [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.3">2Co 11:3</reference>). Last in being, she was first in sin--indeed, she alone was deceived. The subtle serpent knew that she was "the weaker vessel" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>). He therefore tempted her, not Adam. She yielded to the temptations of sense and the deceits of Satan; he, to conjugal love. Hence, in the order of God's judicial sentence, the serpent, the prime offender, stands first; the woman, who was deceived, next; and the man, persuaded by his wife, last (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14-Gen.3.19">Ge 3:14-19</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>, Adam is represented as the first transgressor; but there no reference is made to Eve, and Adam is regarded as the head of the sinning race. Hence, as here, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>, woman's "subjection" is represented as the consequence of her being deceived.<div eID="gen37208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being deceived--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the compound Greek verb for the simple, "Having been seduced by deceit": implying how completely Satan succeeded in deceiving her.<div eID="gen37209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was in the transgression--</hi>Greek, "came to be in the transgression": became involved in the existing state of transgression, literally, "the going beyond a command"; breach of a positive precept (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.15">Ro 4:15</reference>). <div eID="gen37210" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeb14ceb91bc931e5e178f8bca7191c3ca4c1c62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18090"/><div sID="gen37211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18090"/><hi type="bold">15. be saved in childbearing--</hi>Greek, "in (literally, 'through') (her, literally, 'the') child-bearing." Through, or by, is often so used to express not the means of her salvation, but the circumstances AMIDST which it has place. Thus <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">1Co 3:15</reference>, "He ... shall be saved: yet so as by (literally, 'through,' that is, amidst) fire": in spite of the fiery ordeal which he has necessarily to pass through, he shall be saved. So here, "In spite of the trial of childbearing which she passes through (as her portion of the curse, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>, 'in sorrow shalt thou bring forth children'), she shall be saved." Moreover, I think it is implied indirectly that the very curse will be turned into a condition favorable to her salvation, by her faithfully performing her part in doing and suffering what God has assigned to her, namely, child-bearing and home duties, her sphere, as distinguished from public teaching, which is not hers, but man's (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). In this home sphere, not ordinarily in one of active duty for advancing the kingdom of God, which contradicts the position assigned to her by God, she will be saved on the same terms as all others, namely, by living faith. Some think that there is a reference to the Incarnation "through THE child-bearing" (Greek), the bearing of the child Jesus. Doubtless this is the ground of women's child-bearing in general becoming to them a blessing, instead of a curse; just as in the original prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">16</reference>) the promise of "the Seed of the woman" (the Saviour) stands in closest connection with the woman's being doomed to "sorrow" in "bringing forth children," her very child-bearing, though in sorrow, being the function assigned to her by God whereby the Saviour was born. This may be an ulterior reference of the Holy Spirit in this verse; but the primary reference required by the context is the one above given. "She shall be saved ([though] with childbearing)," that is, though suffering her part of the primeval curse in childbearing; just as a man shall be saved, though having to bear his part, namely, the sweat of the brow.<div eID="gen37211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if they, &c.--</hi>"if the women (plural, taken out of 'the woman,' <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:14</reference>, which is put for the whole sex) continue," or more literally, "shall (be found at the judgment to) have continued."<div eID="gen37212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith and charity--</hi>the essential way to salvation (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>). Faith is in relation to God. Charity, to our fellow man. Sobriety, to one's self.<div eID="gen37213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sobriety--</hi>"sober-mindedness" (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Ti 2:9</reference>, as contrasted with the unseemly forwardness reproved in <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>). Mental receptivity and activity in family life were recognized in Christianity as the destiny of woman. One reason alleged here by Paul, is the greater danger of self-deception in the weaker sex, and the spread of errors arising from it, especially in a class of addresses in which sober reflectiveness is least in exercise [Neander]. The case (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.9">Ac 21:9</reference>) was doubtless in private, not in public. <chapter eID="1Tim.2"/>

entries.a9f846b0717ae892409413d3121639704ef4f6f7: <div eID="gen51542" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51543" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51544" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51544" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51543" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51545" type="x-p"/> Prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving, must be made for all men; because God will that all should be saved, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1-1Tim.2.4">1Tim 2:1-4</reference>. There is but one God and one Mediator, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5-1Tim.2.7">1Tim 2:5-7</reference>. How men should pray, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Tim 2:8</reference>. How women should adorn themselves, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Tim 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.10">1Tim 2:10</reference>. They are not suffered to teach, nor to nor to usurp authority over men, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.14">1Tim 2:11-14</reference>. How they may expect to be saved in child-bearing, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.15">1Tim 2:15</reference>. <div eID="gen51545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51546" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51547" type="x-p"/> I exhort - that, first of all - Prayer for the pardon of sin, and for obtaining necessary supplies of grace, and continual protection from God, with gratitude and thanksgiving for mercies already received, are duties which our sinful and dependent state renders absolutely necessary; and which should be chief in our view, and first of all performed. It is difficult to know the precise difference between the four words used here by the apostle. They are sometimes distinguished thus: - <div eID="gen51547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51548" type="x-p"/> Supplications - Δεησεις· Prayers for averting evils of every kind. <div eID="gen51548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51549" type="x-p"/> Prayers - Προσευχας· Prayers for obtaining the good things, spiritual and temporal, which ourselves need. <div eID="gen51549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51550" type="x-p"/> Intercessions - Εντευξεις· Prayers in behalf of others. <div eID="gen51550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51551" type="x-p"/> Giving of thanks - Ευχαριστιας· Praises to God, as the parent of all good, for all the blessings which we and others have received. It is probable that the apostle gives directions here for public worship; and that the words may be thus paraphrased: "Now, I exhort first of all that, in the public assemblies, deprecations of evils, and supplications for such good things as are necessary, and intercessions for their conversion, and thanksgiving for mercies, be offered in behalf of all men - for heathens as well as for Christians, and for enemies as well as for friends." See Macknight.
entries.a05e4e1c11aac93ef06a7fb43708ae68fd4ecdef: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51552" type="x-p"/> For kings - As it is a positive maxim of Christianity to pray for all secular governors, so it has ever been the practice of Christians. When St. Cyprian defended himself before the Roman proconsul, he said: Hunc (Deum) deprecamur-pro nobis et pro omnibus hominibus; et pro incolumitate ipsorum Imperatorum. "We pray to God, not only for ourselves, but for all mankind, and particularly for the emperors." Tertullian, in his Apology, is more particular: Oramus pro omnibus Imperatoribus, vitam illis prolixam, imperium securum, domum tutam, exercitus fortes, senatum fidelem, populum probum, orbem quietum, et quaecunque hominis et Caesaris vota sunt. Apol., cap. 30. "We pray for all the emperors, that God may grant them long life, a secure government, a prosperous family, vigorous troops, a faithful senate, an obedient people; that the whole world may be in peace; and that God may grant, both to Caesar and to every man, the accomplishment of their just desires." <div eID="gen51552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51553" type="x-p"/> So Origen: Ευχομεθα τους βασιλεις και αρχοντας μετα της βασιλικης δυναμεως και σωφρονα τον λογισμον εχοντας εὑρεθηναι. Cont. Cels., lib. viii. "We pray for kings and rulers, that with their royal authority they may be found possessing a wise and prudent mind." Indeed they prayed even for those by whom they were persecuted. If the state be not in safety, the individual cannot be secure; self-preservation, therefore, should lead men to pray for the government under which they live. Rebellions and insurrections seldom terminate even in political good; and even where the government is radically bad, revolutions themselves are most precarious and hazardous. They who wish such commotions would not be quiet under the most mild and benevolent government. <div eID="gen51553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51554" type="x-p"/> That we may lead a quiet and peaceable life - We thus pray for the government that the public peace may be preserved. Good rulers have power to do much good; we pray that their authority may be ever preserved and well directed. Bad rulers have power to do much evil; we pray that they may be prevented from thus using their power. So that, whether the rulers be good or bad, prayer for them is the positive duty of all Christians; and the answer to their prayers, in either ease, will be the means of their being enabled to lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
entries.d67c3d594360da2fc337365b260ab296f52f5db1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51555" type="x-p"/> This is good and acceptable - Prayer for all legally constituted authorities is good in itself, because useful to ourselves and to the public at large, and it is acceptable in the sight of God our Savior; and this is its highest sanction and its highest character: it is good; it is well pleasing to God.
entries.1eb782cbf3ec2ddee7435d28f917b0e0646686b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51556" type="x-p"/> Who will have all men to be saved - Because he wills the salvation of all men; therefore, he wills that all men should be prayed for. In the face of such a declaration, how can any Christian soul suppose that God ever unconditionally and eternally reprobated any man? Those who can believe so, one would suppose, can have little acquaintance either with the nature of God, or the bowels of Christ. <div eID="gen51556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51557" type="x-p"/> And to come unto the knowledge of the truth - The truth - the Gospel of Christ, should be proclaimed to them; and it is the duty of all who know it, to diffuse it far and wide, and when it is made known, then it is the duty of those who hear it to acknowledge and receive it. This is the proper import of the original word, that they may come, εις επιγνωσιν αληθειας, to the acknowledgment of the truth - that they may receive it as the truth, and make it the rule of their faith, the model and director of their life and actions.
entries.54209cde8bc853a73982f92849a87ed9403efcf5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51558" type="x-p"/> There is one God - Who is the maker, governor, and preserver of all men, of every condition, and of every nation, and equally wills the salvation of all. <div eID="gen51558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51559" type="x-p"/> And one mediator - The word μεσιτης, mediator, signifies, literally, a middle person, one whose office it is to reconcile two parties at enmity; and hence Suidas explains it by ειρηνοποιος, a peace-maker. God was offended with the crimes of men; to restore them to his peace, Jesus Christ was incarnated; and being God and man, both God and men met in and were reconciled by him. But this reconciliation required a sacrifice on the part of the peace-maker or mediator; hence what follows.
entries.d9e2952e67fc55f2b43c2c82b82e8c035899a12f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51560" type="x-p"/> Who gave himself a ransom - The word λυτρον signifies a ransom paid for the redemption of a captive; and αντιλυτρον, the word used here, and applied to the death of Christ, signifies that ransom which consists in the exchange of one person for another, or the redemption of life by life; or, as Schleusner has expressed it in his translation of these words, Qui morte sua omnes liberavit a vitiositatis vi et poenis, a servitute quassi et miseria peccatorum. "He who by his death has redeemed all from the power and punishment of vice, from the slavery and misery of sinners." As God is the God and father of all, (for there is but one God, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Tim 2:5</reference>), and Jesus Christ the mediator of all, so he gave himself a ransom for all; i.e., for all that God made, consequently for every human soul; unless we could suppose that there are human souls of which God is not the Creator; for the argument of the apostle is plainly this: <div eID="gen51560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51561" type="x-p"/> 1. There is one God; <div eID="gen51561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51562" type="x-p"/> 2. This God is the Creator of all; <div eID="gen51562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51563" type="x-p"/> 3. He has made a revelation of his kindness to all; <div eID="gen51563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51564" type="x-p"/> 4. He will have all men to be saved, and come unto the knowledge of the truth; and <div eID="gen51564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51565" type="x-p"/> 5. He has provided a mediator for all, who has given himself a ransom for all. As surely as God has created all men, so surely has Jesus Christ died for all men. This is a truth which the nature and revelation of God unequivocally proclaim. <div eID="gen51565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51566" type="x-p"/> To be testified in due time - The original words, το μαρτυριον καιροις ιδιοις, are not very clear, and have been understood variously. The most authentic copies of the printed Vulgate have simply, Testimonium temporibus suis; which Calmet translates: Rendant ainsi temoignage au tems marqu; "Thus rendering testimony at the appointed time." Dr. Macknight thus: Of which the testimony is in its proper season. Wakefield thus: "That testimony reserved to its proper time" Rosenmullen: Haec est doctrina, temporibus suis reservata. "This is the doctrine which is reserved for its own times;" that is, adds he, quoe suo tempore in omni terrarum orbe tradetur, "the doctrine which in its own time shall be delivered to all the inhabitants of the earth." Here he translates μαρτυριον, doctrine; and contends that this, not testimony, is its meaning, not only in this passage, but in <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">1Cor 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">1Cor 2:1</reference>, etc. Instead of μαρτυριον, testimony, one MS., Cod. Kk., vi. 4, in the public library, Cambridge, has, μυστηριον, mystery; but this is not acknowledged by any other MS., nor by any version. In D*FG the whole clause is read thus: οὑ το μαρτυριον καιροις ιδιοις εδοθη· The testimony of which was given in its own times. This is nearly the reading which was adopted in the first printed copies of the Vulgate. One of them now before me reads the passage thus: Cujus testimonium temporibus suis confirmatum est. "The testimony of which is confirmed in its own times." This reading was adopted by Pope Sixtus V., in the famous edition published by him; but was corrected to the reading above, by Pope Clement VIII. And this was rendered literally by our first translator: Whos witnessinge is confermyd in his timis. This appears to be the apostle's meaning: Christ gave himself a ransom for all. This, in the times which seemed best to the Divine wisdom, was to be testified to every nation, and people, and tongue. The apostles had begun this testimony; and, in the course of the Divine economy, it has ever since been gradually promulgated; and at present runs with a more rapid course than ever.
entries.efa531c611a7edd4025bdd165329f882336fa944: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51567" type="x-p"/> I am ordained a preacher - I am set apart, ετεθην, appointed. The word does not imply any imposition of hands by either bishop or presbytery, as is vulgarly supposed. <div eID="gen51567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51568" type="x-p"/> I speak the truth in Christ - As I have received my commission from him, so I testify his truth. I did not run before I was sent; and I speak nothing but what I have received. <div eID="gen51568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51569" type="x-p"/> A teacher of the Gentiles - Being specially commissioned to preach the Gospel, not to the Jews, but to the nations of the world. <div eID="gen51569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51570" type="x-p"/> In faith and verity - Faithfully and truly; preaching the Truth, the whole Truth, and nothing but the Truth; and this fervently, affectionately, and perseveringly. <div eID="gen51570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51571" type="x-p"/> Instead of εν πιστει, in faith, the Cod. Alexand. has εν πνευματι, in spirit. "A teacher of the Gentiles in spirit and truth."
entries.f9a49adbb0651ec5e663f1a5f74e4a77e2656fae: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51572" type="x-p"/> I will therefore - Seeing the apostle had his authority from Christ, and spoke nothing but what he received from him, his βουλομαι, I will, is equal to I command. <div eID="gen51572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51573" type="x-p"/> That men pray - That is, for the blessings promised in this testimony of God. For, although God has provided them, yet he will not give them to such as will not pray. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Tim 2:1</reference>, the subject of which is here resumed. <div eID="gen51573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51574" type="x-p"/> Everywhere - Εν παντι τοπῳ· In every place. That they should always have a praying heart, and this will ever find a praying place. This may refer to a Jewish superstition. They thought, at first, that no prayer could be acceptable that was not offered at the temple at Jerusalem; afterward this was extended to the Holy Land; but, when they became dispersed among the nations, they built oratories or places of prayer, principally by rivers and by the seaside; and in these they were obliged to allow that public prayer might be legally offered, but nowhere else. In opposition to this, the apostle, by the authority of Christ, commands men to pray everywhere; that all places belong to God's dominions; and, as he fills every place, in every place he may be worshipped and glorified. As to ejaculatory prayer, they allowed that this might be performed standing, sitting, leaning, lying, walking by the way, and during their labor. Beracoth, fol. xi. 1. And yet in some other places they teach differently. See Schoettgen. <div eID="gen51574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51575" type="x-p"/> Lifting up holy hands - It was a common custom, not only among the Jews, but also among the heathens, to lift up or spread out their arms and hands in prayer. It is properly the action of entreaty and request; and seems to be an effort to embrace the assistance requested. But the apostle probably alludes to the Jewish custom of laying their hands on the head of the animal which they brought for a sin-offering, confessing their sins, and then giving up the life of the animal as an expiation for the sins thus confessed. And this very notion is conveyed in the original term επαιροντας, from αιρω to lift up, and επι, upon or over. This shows us how Christians should pray. They should come to the altar; set God before their eyes; humble themselves for their sins; bring as a sacrifice the Lamb of God; lay their hands on this sacrifice; and by faith offer it to God in their souls' behalf, expecting salvation through his meritorious death alone. <div eID="gen51575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51576" type="x-p"/> Without wrath - Having no vindictive feeling against any person; harbouring no unforgiving spirit, while they are imploring pardon for their own offenses. <div eID="gen51576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51577" type="x-p"/> The holy hands refer to the Jewish custom of washing their hands before prayer; this was done to signify that they had put away all sin, and purposed to live a holy life. <div eID="gen51577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51578" type="x-p"/> And doubting - Διαλογισμου or διαλογισμων, as in many MSS., reasonings, dialogues. Such as are often felt by distressed penitents and timid believers; faith, hope, and unbelief appearing to hold a disputation and controversy in their own bosoms, in the issue of which unbelief ordinarily triumphs. The apostle therefore wills them to come, implicitly relying on the promises of God, and the sacrifice and mediation of Jesus Christ.
entries.879269313ae0cc3f831da820a798de60aae56b95: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51579" type="x-p"/> In like manner also - That is, he wills or commands what follows, as he had commanded what went before. <div eID="gen51579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51580" type="x-p"/> That women adorn themselves - Και τας γυναικας ες καταστολῃ κοσμιῳ. The apostle seems to refer here to different parts of the Grecian and Roman dress. The στολη, stola, seems to have been originally very simple. It was a long piece of cloth, doubled in the middle, and sewed up on both sides, leaving room only for the arms; at the top, a piece was cut out, or a slit made, through which the head passed. It hung down to the feet, both before and behind, and was girded with the zona round the body, just under the breasts. It was sometimes made with, sometimes without, sleeves; and, that it might sit the better, it was gathered on each shoulder with a band or buckle. Some of the Greek women wore them open on each side, from the bottom up above the knee, so as to discover a part of the thigh. These were termed φαινομηριδες, showers (discoverers) of the thigh; but it was, in general, only young girls or immodest women who wore them thus. <div eID="gen51580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51581" type="x-p"/> The καταστολη seems to have been the same as the pallium or mantle, which, being made nearly in the form of the stola, hung down to the waist, both in back and front, was gathered on the shoulder with a band or buckle, had a hole or slit at top for the head to pass through, and hung loosely over the stola, without being confined by the zona or girdle. Representations of these dresses may be seen in Lens' Costume des Peuples de l'Antiquit, fig. 11, 12, 13, and 16. A more modest and becoming dress than the Grecian was never invented; it was, in a great measure, revived in England about the year 1805, and in it, simplicity, decency, and elegance were united; but it soon gave place to another mode, in which frippery and nonsense once more prevailed. It was too rational to last long; and too much like religious simplicity to be suffered in a land of shadows, and a world of painted outsides. <div eID="gen51581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51582" type="x-p"/> With shamefacedness and sobriety - The stola, catastola, girdle, etc., though simple in themselves, were often highly ornamented both with gold and precious stones; and, both among the Grecian and Roman women, the hair was often crisped and curled in the most variegated and complex manner. To this the apostle alludes when he says: Μη εν πλεγμασιν, η χρυσῳ, η μαργαριταις, η ἱματισμῳ πολυτελει· Not with plaited hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly raiment. The costly raiment might refer to the materials out of which the raiment was made, and to the workmanship; the gold and pearls, to the ornaments on the raiment. <div eID="gen51582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51583" type="x-p"/> With shame-facedness or modesty, μετα αιδους. This would lead them to avoid every thing unbecoming or meretricious in the mode or fashion of their dress. <div eID="gen51583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51584" type="x-p"/> With sobriety, μετα σωφροσυνης. Moderation would lead them to avoid all unnecessary expense. They might follow the custom or costume of the country as to the dress itself, for nothing was ever more becoming than the Grecian stola, catastola, and zona; but they must not imitate the extravagance of those who, through impurity or littleness of mind, decked themselves merely to attract the eye of admiration, or set in lying action the tongue of flattery. Woman has been invidiously defined: An animal fond of dress. How long will they permit themselves to be thus degraded? <div eID="gen51584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51585" type="x-p"/> Those beautiful lines of Homer, in which he speaks of the death of Euphorbus, who was slain by Menelaus, show how anciently the Grecians plaited and adorned their hair: - Αντικρυ δ' απαλοιο δι' αυχενος ηλυθ' ακωκη· Δουπησεν δε πεσων, αραβησε δε τευχε' επ' αυτῳ. Αἱματι οἱ δευοντο κομαι, Χαριτεσσιν ὁμοιαι, Πλοχμοι θ' οἱ χρυσῳ τε και αργυρῳ εσφηκωντο. <div eID="gen51585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51586" type="x-p"/> Il. xvii., ver. 49. <div eID="gen51586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51587" type="x-p"/> Wide through the neck appears the ghastly wound; <div eID="gen51587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51588" type="x-p"/> Prone sinks the warrior, and his arms rebound. <div eID="gen51588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51589" type="x-p"/> The shining circlets of his golden hair, <div eID="gen51589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51590" type="x-p"/> Which e'en the Graces might be proud to wear, <div eID="gen51590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51591" type="x-p"/> Instarr'd with gems and gold bestrew the shore, <div eID="gen51591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51592" type="x-p"/> With dust dishonor'd, and deform'd with gore. <div eID="gen51592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51593" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen51593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51594" type="x-p"/> Or thus, more literally: - <div eID="gen51594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51595" type="x-p"/> Sounding he fell; loud rang his batter'd arms. <div eID="gen51595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51596" type="x-p"/> His locks, which e'en the Graces might have own'd, <div eID="gen51596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51597" type="x-p"/> Blood sullied, and his ringlets wound about <div eID="gen51597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51598" type="x-p"/> With twine of gold and silver, swept the dust. <div eID="gen51598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51599" type="x-p"/> Cowper. <div eID="gen51599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51600" type="x-p"/> The extravagance to which the Grecian and Asiatic women went in their ornaments might well be a reason for the apostle's command. <div eID="gen51600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51601" type="x-p"/> Kypke, however, denies that any particular article of dress is intended here, and says that καταστολη is to be understood as coming from καταστελλω, to restrain, repress; and he refers it to that government of the mind, or moderation which women should exercise over their dress and demeanour in general, and every thing that may fall under the observation of the senses. All this, undoubtedly, the apostle had in view. <div eID="gen51601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51602" type="x-p"/> When either women or men spend much time, cost, and attention on decorating their persons, it affords a painful proof that within there is little excellence, and that they are endeavoring to supply the want of mind and moral good by the feeble and silly aids of dress and ornament. Were religion out of the question, common sense would say in all these things: Be decent; but be moderate and modest.
entries.cf8d6673d2c3b80562456a2aa09a7767dc4cb427: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51603" type="x-p"/> But (which becometh, etc. - That is: Good works are the only ornaments with which women professing Christianity should seek to be adorned. The Jewish matrons were accustomed to cry to the bride: "There is no need of paint, no need of antimony, no need of braided hair; she herself is most beautiful." The eastern women use a preparation of antimony, which they apply both to the eyes and eyelids, and by which the eye itself acquires a wonderful lustre.
entries.6b3dbcde7d7dac81e3c22b015d67a6876065e701: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51604" type="x-p"/> Let the woman learn in silence - This is generally supposed to be a prohibition of women's preaching. I have already said what I judge necessary on this subject in the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.5">1Cor 11:5</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Cor 14:34</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">1Cor 14:35</reference> (note); to which places I beg leave to refer the reader.
entries.a234efa9b1aa0613f213105d2e91117e30246e80: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51605" type="x-p"/> Nor to usurp authority - A woman should attempt nothing, either in public or private, that belongs to man as his peculiar function. This was prohibited by the Roman laws: In multis juris nostri articulis deterior est conditio foeminarum quam masculorun,; l. 9, Pap. Lib. 31, Quaest. Foeminoe ab omnibus officiis civilibus vel publicis remotae sunt; et ideo nec judicis esse possunt, nec magistratum gerere, nec postulare, nec pro alio invenire, nec procuratores existere; l. 2, de Reg. Juris. Ulp. Lib. i. Ad Sab. - Vid. Poth. Pand. Justin., vol. i. p. 13. "In our laws the condition of women is, in many respects, worse than that of men. Women are precluded from all public offices; therefore they cannot be judges, nor execute the function of magistrates; they cannot sue, plead, nor act in any case, as proxies." They were under many other disabilities, which may be seen in different places of the Pandects. <div eID="gen51605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51606" type="x-p"/> But to be in silence - It was lawful for men in public assemblies to ask questions, or even interrupt the speaker when there was any matter in his speech which they did not understand; but this liberty was not granted to women. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Cor 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">1Cor 14:35</reference> (note).
entries.2151a6b724204bc0d8ec071fc35e922f80cf3732: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen51606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51607" type="x-p"/> For Adam was first formed, then Eve - And by this very act God designed that he should have the pre-eminence. God fitted man, by the robust construction of his body, to live a public life, to contend with difficulties, and to be capable of great exertions. The structure of woman's body plainly proves that she was never designed for those exertions required in public life. In this the chief part of the natural inferiority of woman is to be sought.
entries.af71495adcd2a45001d3373a26284c8bacfc446f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen51607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51608" type="x-p"/> Adam was not deceived - It does not appear that Satan attempted the man; the woman said: The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat. Adam received the fruit from the hand of his wife; he knew he was transgressing, he was not deceived; however, she led the way, and in consequence of this she was subjected to the domination of her husband: Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee; <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen 3:16</reference>. There is a Greek verse, but it is not English law, that speaks a language nearly similar to that above: - Γυναικι δ' αρχειν ου διδωσιν ἡ φυσις. <div eID="gen51608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51609" type="x-p"/> For nature suffers not a woman's rule. <div eID="gen51609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51610" type="x-p"/> God has not only rendered her unfit for it, but he has subjected her, expressly, to the government of the man.
entries.a8afe77eae80bf9bd2ee421825b8ea7f9685ebde: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen51610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51611" type="x-p"/> She shalt be saved in child-bearing - Σωθησεται δε δια της τεκνογονιας· She shall be saved through child-bearing - she shall be saved by means, or through the instrumentality, of child-bearing or of bringing forth a child. Amidst the different opinions given of the meaning of this very singular text, that of Dr. Macknight appears to me the most probable, which I shall give in his paraphrase and note. "However, though Eve was first in the transgression, and brought death on herself, her husband, and all her posterity, the female sex shall be saved (equally with the male) through child-bearing - through bringing forth the Savior, if they live in faith, and love, and chastity, with that sobriety which I have been recommending. "The word σωθησεται, saved, in this verse refers to ἡ γυνη, the woman, in the foregoing verse, which is certainly Eve. But the apostle did not mean to say that she alone was to be saved through child-bearing, but that all her posterity, whether male or female, are to be saved through the child-bearing of a woman; as is evident from his adding, If they live in faith and love and holiness, with sobriety. For safety in child-bearing does not depend on that condition at all; since many pious women die in child-bearing, while others of a contrary character are preserved. The salvation of the human race, through child-bearing, was intimated in the sentence passed on the serpent, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen 3:15</reference> : I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed. It shall bruise thy head. Accordingly, the Savior being conceived in the womb of his mother by the power of the Holy Ghost, he is truly the seed of the woman who was to bruise the head of the serpent; and a woman, by bringing him forth, has been the occasion of our salvation." This is the most consistent sense, for in the way in which it is commonly understood it does not apply. There are innumerable instances of women dying in child-bed who have lived in faith and charity and holiness, with sobriety; and equally numerous instances of worthless women, slaves to different kinds of vices, who have not only been saved in child-bearing, but have passed through their travail with comparatively little pain; hence that is not the sense in which we should understand the apostle.
